extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, regulators, administrative law attorneys, law professors, and engaged citizens interested in regulatory design and reform
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for designing and evaluating government regulation consistent with the rule of law, contrasted with a cost‑benefit/physician model of regulation. Emphasizes legal (statutory and constitutional) compliance, institutional separation, and policy design tradeoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physician's five-step policymaking process
rubrics_metrics.description: Policymakers should follow a five-step process analogous to a physician: (1) identify the symptom (the adverse condition), (2) diagnose the disease (cause of the symptom), (3) identify alternative remedies, (4) assess costs and benefits (including side effects and effectiveness) of each remedy, and (5) select the remedy that provides the greatest net benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this structured approach to regulatory decisionmaking to compare alternatives efficiently; consider effectiveness, monetary cost, side effects, and select the option that maximizes net welfare. The reviewer notes this can become complex and costly and should be used cost‑effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize the sum of error and decision costs
rubrics_metrics.description: A rule of thumb for choosing regulatory directives: craft directives to minimize the combined (sum) of error costs (harms from prohibiting beneficial conduct or permitting harmful conduct) and decision costs (costs of drafting, interpreting, complying with, and enforcing nuanced rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize trade-offs: more nuance can reduce error costs but increase decision costs for regulators, regulated parties, and adjudicators. The chosen regulatory form should balance these to maximize net social welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-effective information gathering across regulatory alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Policymakers should gather only as much welfare-related information as can be cost‑effectively collected on all potential regulatory options, then select the option that minimizes the sum of error and decision costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider opportunity costs of selecting one regulatory approach over others; avoid exhaustive data collection that is not cost‑justified. Use information sufficient to compare alternatives rather than attempting impossible omniscience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of regulation (scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation is defined as 'any threat-backed governmental directive aimed at fixing a defect in “private ordering”' (i.e., governmental directives to correct market failures), explicitly excluding common-law private ordering (property, tort, contract).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this working definition when deciding whether a governmental action is a regulation subject to regulatory analysis; recognize it centers on top‑down, threat-backed directives rather than private-law arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the physician's approach to specific market failures
rubrics_metrics.description: When addressing common justifications for regulation—unwanted economic externalities; public goods; excessive market power; information asymmetry; agency costs (from market power/information asymmetry); and cognitive/behavioral limitations—policymakers should identify symptoms, diagnose sources, catalogue remedies, assess costs/benefits, and select the remedy minimizing error+decision costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each type of defect, discuss symptoms, sources, remedies; some remedies may only alleviate symptoms while others target root causes. Evaluate alternatives comparatively rather than defaulting to regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory forbearance as a legitimate option
rubrics_metrics.description: In many cases the optimal remedy may be to do nothing: regulatory forbearance should be considered as a potential, sometimes preferable, response to identified problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid presumption that new regulation is necessary; evaluate whether private ordering or existing rules can address the issue before imposing new directives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full statutory compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations and the procedures to enact and apply them must be in complete and consistent compliance with all applicable congressional statutes and controlling court decisions interpreting those statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where components of the regulatory system do not meet statutory standards, legislative or executive reforms should be formulated to bring the system into conformity with statute and precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional compliance (original public meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond statutory compliance, regulations must conform to the Constitution as interpreted according to its original public meaning; regulatory lawfulness requires consistency with fundamental constitutional structure and limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess regulations against separation of powers, enumerated powers, and other constitutional constraints; prefer reforms that align regulatory practice with original‑meaning constitutional controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of functions and institutional independence
rubrics_metrics.description: A lawful regulatory system requires clearly separate branches performing legislation, executive administration, and adjudication, each operating transparently and with essential independence within its constitutional sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislatures should enact general prospective rules, executives should faithfully execute them, and judiciaries should be insulated to interpret and apply laws; avoid consolidating legislative, executive and adjudicative functions within unaccountable agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prospective legislative rulemaking and stability
rubrics_metrics.description: In the legislature, elected representatives enact new rules prospectively; once enacted, those rules should remain fixed unless amended by the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stability and predictability of law are essential; avoid regulatory practices that create constantly changing rules or retroactive rulemaking that undermine predictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive fidelity to legislative enactments
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive branch is charged with faithfully executing and administering the rules enacted by the legislature rather than effectively creating new substantive law through agency action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory actions should implement legislative commands rather than expand policy through loosely defined discretion; this preserves separation of powers and legality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial insulation and retroactive application to disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: The judiciary should be insulated from politics and charged with interpreting enacted rules and applying them retroactively to resolve past disputes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should apply laws as written and act as neutral arbiters rather than as policy‑making bodies; this supports the rule of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws must be readily accessible and intelligible
rubrics_metrics.description: For a system to embody the rule of law, laws and legal institutions must be readily accessible and intelligible to the persons covered by them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft regulations and procedures so that regulated parties can understand obligations and plan accordingly; avoid opaque, obscure, or overly technical rules that undermine notice and compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat like cases alike; apply laws as written
rubrics_metrics.description: The legal system should treat like cases alike and faithfully apply laws as written without exception or waiver to adjudicate questions of right and liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid selective enforcement, ad hoc waivers, or inconsistent application that create unpredictability and arbitrary outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and protect fundamental human rights, including property rights
rubrics_metrics.description: A lawful regulatory system must recognize and respect fundamental human rights—including property rights—and protect those rights from arbitrary actions by private parties and public officials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulators should refrain from redistributive or liberty‑infringing measures absent clear statutory authorization and constitutional legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proscriptive regulatory approach (clear prohibitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under a rule‑of‑law approach, regulation should proscribe actions inconsistent with objectives (explicit prohibitions); anything not specifically prohibited should be permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This proscriptive approach enhances foreseeability and allows private ordering and innovation within the 'open spaces' where conduct is not banned; prefer clear limits over broad affirmative micromanagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid politicized, arbitrary regulatory practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory lawfulness requires avoidance of practices like politicized enforcement, retroactivity, waivers, picking winners and losers, and broadly defined discretionary authority that create uncertainty and arbitrariness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design rules and procedures to limit agency discretion that leads to backdoor policymaking and unequal treatment; emphasize transparency, accountability, and procedural regularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution on social welfare modeling and measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Social welfare modeling (choosing a social welfare function and quantifying quality‑of‑life inputs) is inherently subjective and relies on unverifiable assumptions; it can lend false legitimacy to policy choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policymakers should be skeptical of models that purport to objectively measure social welfare; recognize the limits of GDP and aggregated models and the role of value judgments in modeling inputs and outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defer to persons possessing context-specific information
rubrics_metrics.description: Because context‑specific information relevant to resource allocation is widely dispersed, the best information often resides with the individuals and market participants directly affected rather than with central regulators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate local/industry knowledge and the perspectives of regulated parties into analysis; be wary of relying primarily on regional regulator offices for context‑specific data. Deference to those with practical, on‑the‑ground knowledge can improve regulatory outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote transparency, predictability, and rule‑of‑law features to support prosperity and liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: A system of governance based on rule‑of‑law attributes (clear, stable, knowable rules; constrained discretion; respect for property and individual rights) facilitates planning, innovation, efficient allocation of resources, and protection of liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize regulatory reforms that increase foreseeability and constrain arbitrary power so individuals and businesses can undertake productive activity with confidence.
